newsitem.title: CHINA: China tells government to stay out of listed firms.
newsitem.headline: China tells government to stay out of listed firms.

text.p: China has issued a circular on the status of listed firms, saying they are independent and must pay no administrative fees to any government department, the Shanghai Securities News said on Tuesday.

The circular, issued by departments headed by the State Commission for Economic Restructuring, said company chairmen must be elected by shareholders and managers must be appointed by the board of directors, and no government department has the authority to appoint any top official of listed firms.
Public servants cannot be the chairmen or managers of listed firms, and those who want to be company officials must resign their public posts, the circular said.
China revived its stock market and listed firms in the late 1980s. Most of the listed firms were former state-run enterprises.

In theory, the firms are independent. But in practice, government departments continue to interfere in their activities, including charging administration fees or appointing senior officials, Chinese stock analysts say.
The circular also ordered listed firms to buy back so-called "legal person shares" that had been illegally sold or given to individuals. The shares, owned by institutions, are non-tradeable.

Beijing has banned firms from selling such shares to individuals, but some companies have sold them at low prices or distributed them free of charge to staff members as a form of welfare, the analysts said.
This has also led to limited black market trading in these non-tradable shares, they said.
"Listed companies or holders of legal person shares should buy back the legal person shares in the hands of individuals," the circular was quoted as saying.
"If a company or legal person shareholders cannot afford to buy them back, the shares owned by retail investors should be collected and be entrusted to a securities house," it said.
